title: Discrete-event simulation
summary: Discrete-event simulation models a system as a sequence of instantaneous events that change system state, advancing a clock to the next event time rather than simulating every moment. It contrasts with continuous simulation by using discrete state changes and differential equations. The core mechanism involves maintaining a pending event list, typically a priority queue sorted chronologically, where each event triggers follow-up events or state updates. Common components include a clock, state variables, random-number generators for stochastic inputs, and statistics collectors. A typical example models a queueing system, such as bank customers and a teller, where arrivals, service starts, and service ends dynamically schedule subsequent events. The simulation must define an ending condition, as it could otherwise run indefinitely due to bootstrapping, where initial event times are not yet representative of the steady-state distribution.

mechanisms.title: Event scheduling via priority queue
mechanisms.explanation: The simulation maintains a pending event list organized as a priority queue sorted by event time. Regardless of insertion order, events are removed and processed in strict chronological order. This structure ensures that the simulation clock advances to the next event start time, skipping idle intervals, and that each event code executes its state changes and schedules follow-up events.

mechanisms.title: Bootstrapping for steady-state initialization
mechanisms.explanation: Because initial pending events may not reflect the steady-state distribution, the model is bootstrapped by running briefly and discarding early output. Over time, the scheduling of additional events causes the event-time distribution to converge toward steady state. Statistics are then gathered only after this bootstrapping phase or after sufficient runtime overwhelms the initial conditions.
